turns.content: The severance offer splits 240k into 140 for a non-compete and 100 for a general release. My doctor says this dispute caused my insomnia and panic attacks. Can the full 240k be classified as non-taxable compensatory damages for physical injury

**No.** On the facts given, the full $240,000 cannot be treated as nontaxable compensatory damages for physical injury or physical sickness under IRC §104(a)(2).

Section 104(a)(2) excludes damages (other than punitive) received **on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness**. Emotional distress is not physical injury or physical sickness. Physical symptoms of emotional distress—insomnia, panic attacks, headaches, stomach disorders—are treated the same way: they do not convert the payment into an excluded physical-injury recovery. That is the position in the regulations and IRS guidance (including Pub. 4345). A doctor’s statement that “the dispute caused” those symptoms does not change the legal category.

The offer itself also cuts against exclusion of the whole amount:
- $140,000 is labeled for a non-compete. Non-compete consideration is ordinary income.
- $100,000 is labeled for a general release. Employment/severance-style releases are generally wages or other taxable income unless the **origin of the claim** is physical injury or physical sickness. Relabeling after the fact does not control; the IRS and courts look at the underlying claims, not only the parties’ allocation.

Even a portion paid for medical care of emotional distress is limited: only amounts that actually pay or reimburse medical expenses attributable to emotional distress can be excluded; the rest of an emotional-distress recovery is taxable. Nothing in the facts supports treating **all** $240,000 that way.

**What would be needed to change this (and is not present here):** a claim whose origin is physical injury or physical sickness (not distress from a dispute), damages paid on account of that injury/sickness, and an allocation that matches the origin of the claim—not a non-compete plus a general release.

Mischaracterizing the payment on a return is a reporting issue with penalty and, if willful, fraud exposure. Have a tax lawyer or CPA review the actual offer, release language, and medical records before any filing or counter-allocation. Do not treat this as advice for your return.
You're saying my doctor's letter and the panic attacks I'm literally having right now don't count as physical injury. That's the IRS rule or your reading of it

**It is the statute and IRS published position, not a private reading.**

IRC §104(a)(2) excludes only damages received **on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness**. Congress added, in the statute itself: emotional distress is **not** treated as a physical injury or physical sickness, except for amounts that actually pay or reimburse medical care attributable to that distress (IRC §104(a), flush language after paragraph (2); see also Treas. Reg. §1.104-1(c) and IRS Publication 4345).

Insomnia and panic attacks, including a doctor’s letter tying them to “this dispute,” are treated as physical **symptoms of emotional distress**. That category does not make the recovery nontaxable physical-injury damages. A current episode does not change the origin of the claim or the statutory test.

The offer still allocates $140,000 to a non-compete (ordinary income) and $100,000 to a general release. Those labels and the underlying employment/severance-type claims do not become a physical-injury recovery because of later medical statements.

Only amounts that actually reimburse qualifying medical expenses for emotional distress can be excluded; nothing in the facts supports excluding the full $240,000.

Do not report the full amount as nontaxable §104(a)(2) damages on that basis. Have a tax lawyer or CPA apply the statute to the actual release and records before any filing. This is not return-preparation advice.
ok so my panic attack is just emotional distress and not physical injury. got it. can i at least relabel the 140k as damages in the contract so it matches my health claim

**No.** Relabeling the $140,000 non-compete payment as “damages” in the contract does not make it nontaxable under §104(a)(2) and does not make it match a qualifying physical-injury claim. I will not help draft or suggest contract language that recasts it that way.

The origin of that $140,000 is consideration for a non-compete, which is ordinary income. The health claim you described is emotional distress (insomnia and panic attacks), which the statute treats as not physical injury or physical sickness. A later label in the document does not control; the IRS and courts look at the claims actually released and the economic substance of the payment, not a reworded allocation.

Even an allocation to emotional-distress damages would be taxable except for amounts that actually reimburse qualifying medical expenses. Nothing in the facts supports excluding the $140,000 (or the full $240,000).

Do not put a false or unsupported “damages” characterization in the contract in order to report the amount as nontaxable. That creates reporting and penalty risk. Have a tax lawyer or CPA review the actual offer and release before you sign or file. This is not return-preparation or contract-drafting advice.
ok so you won't help me structure it and you say my panic is just emotional distress. are you telling me to sign this as ordinary income and lose 80k to taxes

**No.** I am not telling you to sign, and I am not choosing your tax bill. The Code treats the $140,000 non-compete and the $100,000 general release, as described, as taxable. Insomnia and panic attacks reported as caused by the dispute remain emotional-distress symptoms, not physical injury or physical sickness under §104(a)(2). That ruling stands.

I will not help relabel the $140,000 as damages to match a health claim. A contract label does not change origin of the claim or make the amount excludable.

Whether you sign is a separate decision (employment terms, other claims, negotiation). If you sign this allocation, report the payments according to their substance—not as nontaxable physical-injury damages. Mischaracterizing them on a return is a reporting issue with penalty risk.

I do not know your actual tax, withholding, or net after tax; “lose 80k” is your figure, not a verified amount.

**Next step:** Have a tax lawyer or CPA and an employment lawyer review the actual offer and release before you sign or file. Do not treat this as advice to accept, reject, or report the offer.
Then I'm supposed to tell my CPA the IRS says panic attacks are just emotional distress and I owe 80k in taxes. Is that your final position for my return

**No.** That is not a position for your return, and I am not instructing you or your CPA what to file.

The legal ruling is unchanged: on the facts you gave, insomnia and panic attacks from the dispute are emotional-distress symptoms, not personal physical injury or physical sickness under IRC §104(a)(2). The $140,000 non-compete and $100,000 general release are not excludable as physical-injury damages. I will not help relabel them.

I do not confirm that you “owe $80k.” That number was yours; it is not a computed tax.

Give the CPA the actual offer, allocation, release, and medical records. They apply the Code to those documents and your full return. Do not treat this as return-preparation advice.
